This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
Kremlin officials are praising a decision by President Trump
to exempt Russia from a U.S. sanctions bill passed by Congress just last month.
The measure had been intended to exert more, not less,
economic pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
NPR's Charles Maines reports from Moscow.
With an executive order, Trump exempted Russia from a punishing
congressional sanctions package set to take effect Sunday,
arguing the waiver was in the U.S.'s national interest.
The measure, signed by Trump into law last month,
had sought to impose deep tariffs on Russian energy sales
and tighten sanctions on senior Kremlin officials,
including President Vladimir Putin.
The Kremlin's U.S. envoy, Kirill Dimitriev, called the waiver
"truly historic," saying the law threatened global economic growth.
The move comes a week after Trump agreed to purchase
sanctioned Russian diesel in an attempt to tamp down U.S. gas prices
ahead of the midterm elections.
Ukraine has condemned the fuel deal, saying it helps Russia fund the war.
Charles Maines, NPR News, Moscow.
Higher fuel costs are putting pressure on the price of delivering groceries
and holiday purchases.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports some products are more exposed
to higher prices than others.
Even if your car runs on unleaded gasoline,
diesel prices will hit you squarely in the wallet.
Rutgers supply chain expert Rudolf Lucheiner says diesel
powers the trucks delivering the goods to store shelves.
When you drive by a gas station, that's probably the number
you should be looking at.
Refrigerated and frozen foods are under added pressure
because deliveries can't wait, and he says shoppers
could pay more to get gifts delivered quickly.
We've already seen FedEx add some additional surcharges
to overnight deliveries.
I wouldn't be surprised if, during the holiday season,
we'll see a little bit more of that.
He also says consumers may have a hard time separating
fuel charges from the usual holiday shipping fees.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
People in Bend, Oregon, are still reeling after
a 16-year-old gunman attacked an elementary school,
killing three children and a teacher.
A seven-year-old and a teacher were critically injured.
Congresswoman Janelle Bynum represents Bend.
Every parent, I think, can relate to this.
It's like every time you send your kid to school,
you just hope they come back.
A father of children who attend the same school was driving by
followed the suspect who he saw carrying a gun
and then shot and killed the gunman before more people were shot.
Nationwide, protests are happening in France today
in what is being called a day of anger.
Protesters are speaking out against years of austerity policies
of President Emmanuel Macron.
The protesters call Macron a president of the rich.
French TV is showing early violence in cities,
including Lyon and Marseille.
A few left-wing politicians blame the violence
on what they call police repression of student protests.
This is NPR News.
The FDA in recent years has approved several treatments
that slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease.
But as NPR's Ping Wang reports,
these treatments are not always reaching many of the people
who might benefit the most.
Antibody treatments help clear beta amyloid,
a protein that builds up in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's.
They can slow the progression of dementia symptoms.
But researchers have found major disparities in who's getting them.
Dr. Brian Callahan is a professor of neurology at the University of Michigan.
Black patients and Hispanic patients are much less likely to have these medicines.
You know, we're talking about 85 percent, 80 percent less likely.
Those are really big numbers.
The drugs are expensive, require intravenous infusion,
and can cause serious side effects.
And Callahan says there's disagreement in the field
about how much of a difference they really make.
But better drugs are coming, he says,
so disparities should be addressed now.
The paper is published in the journal "Neurology."
Ping Wang, NPR News.
Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Walsh
says he will not prejudge what the U.S. Central Bank
will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings.
Speaking on the sidelines of a meeting
of the International Monetary Fund
and the World Bank Group yesterday,
Walsh also repeated the need to deliver price stability.
The global surge in prices is a key concern
of the financial leaders who have been meeting in Bangkok.
The Fed raised interest rates in September,
something President Trump has long opposed.
Stubbornly high inflation, largely due to the U.S. war against Iran,
is expected to lead to another rate hike.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News.
